source: Fleming & Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition
finding: Correlation measures of confidence and accuracy (Pearson r, gamma, phi) are distorted by response bias. Bias-free options come from signal detection theory: area under the type 2 ROC (AUROC2) and meta-d'. The paper separates metacognitive bias (how confident), sensitivity (do high-confidence trials tend to be correct) and efficiency (sensitivity given task performance).
numbers: Type 2 hit rate = share of high-confidence trials among correct trials; type 2 false alarm rate = share among incorrect trials. The full type 2 ROC is built by sweeping the confidence criterion.
limits: Theory-level review. AUROC2 still depends on task performance; only meta-d'/d' (efficiency) is meant to be performance-independent.
agent_relevance: Our guardrail on stated confidence should score discrimination (AUROC) separately from calibration (ECE) and bias. One number hides which one fails.

source: Fleming & Lau (2014), calibration versus discrimination
finding: Links the human signal-detection measures to the probability-forecasting literature. Calibration (do 70% claims come true 70% of the time) and discrimination (can confidence separate right from wrong) are different and can come apart.
numbers: A person who says 75% on every trial can be perfectly calibrated and have zero discrimination (footnote in Tian et al. 2023 makes the same point for 50% on binary tasks).
limits: Review, no new data.
agent_relevance: A constant stated confidence can look fine on ECE. Always check spread and AUROC.

source: Mazancieux et al. (2020) Is there a G factor for metacognition?
finding: Large-sample test of whether metacognitive ability is shared across domains. Average confidence correlated across tasks. Metacognitive efficiency (meta-d'/d') also correlated across tasks in a hierarchical Bayesian model, even for task pairs whose first-order performance was not correlated. Earlier nulls were probably low power.
numbers: N=181; four 2AFC tasks (episodic memory, semantic memory, executive function, visual perception); 5 of 6 cross-task correlations in meta-d'/d' significant. First-order d' correlations: episodic-semantic r=.23, executive-semantic r=.27, executive-visual r=.21; other pairs not significant after correction.
quote: at least some components of metacognitive efficiency in retrospective confidence are domain general
limits: Single sample; lab 2AFC tasks with retrospective confidence; not open-ended reasoning. Only 'at least some components' are domain general.
agent_relevance: Supports one shared confidence check rather than one per task type, but whether an LLM's monitoring is domain general needs its own test.

source: Magnus & Peresetsky (2022) A statistical explanation of the Dunning-Kruger effect
finding: Argues the Dunning-Kruger pattern (low scorers overestimate, high scorers underestimate) follows from bounded scales plus noise in self-estimates, with no psychological mechanism needed. A tobit model with boundary constraints fits the data almost perfectly.
numbers: Model: predicted grade = true grade + random noise, censored to 0-100. After adjusting for the group mean the gap is random noise, and only its variance is estimated.
limits: A statistical account, not proof that no metacognitive deficit exists. The paper's own reference list includes opposing work (Schlosser et al. 2013; McIntosh et al. 2019), not opened here.
agent_relevance: Bucketed over/under-estimation plots are weak evidence that a model 'does not know what it does not know'. Use per-item discrimination (AUROC).

source: Kruger & Dunning (1999) Unskilled and unaware of it (as described by Magnus & Peresetsky 2022)
finding: Original claim: low-ability people overestimate performance and lack the metacognitive skill to see it. Recorded only as summarised by the 2022 critique; the original paper was not opened.
limits: Not opened. Contested by the statistical-artifact account (b04).
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'weak models are blind to their weakness' as settled from this effect alone.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Larger pretrained models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false items when the format is right. Models can judge their own sampled answers as P(True), and this improves when they see several of their own samples first. A trained P(IK) head predicts whether the model knows the answer but calibrates poorly on new tasks.
numbers: Models 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B. Calibration improves with size. 20-shot P(True) on five sampling tasks (TriviaQA, Lambada, arithmetic, GSM8k, HumanEval): keeping only answers with P(True)>0.5 raises accuracy on every task.
limits: Pre-RLHF-era models; P(IK) needs training and generalises only partly; format sensitive.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that a model's judgement of its own answer carries signal. Show several samples before asking for P(True).

source: Kadavath et al. (2022), format sensitivity
finding: Replacing one answer option with 'none of the above' harms both accuracy and calibration. RLHF policy miscalibration can be repaired by temperature tuning. P(IK) rises when relevant source text or a hint is in context.
numbers: 52B model on MMLU and BIG-Bench multiple choice; calibration generally improves with model size and capability.
limits: Out-of-distribution P(IK) calibration weaker than in-distribution; ranking transfers better than calibration.
agent_relevance: Confidence is format-fragile. Re-estimate it after retrieval or hints are added, and keep answer formats stable.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Systematic test of black-box confidence: verbalized confidence, sampling consistency, and combinations, on five LLMs and eight tasks. Verbalized confidence is overconfident. Human-inspired prompts reduce ECE but failure prediction stays near chance.
numbers: Vanilla verbalized: GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna average ECE above 0.377; GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% (chance 50%). AUROC rises about 22.2% from GPT-3 to GPT-4. GSM8K GPT-4: 93.6% accuracy, ECE 0.064 by saying 100% on everything.
limits: ECE can be gamed by a constant answer. Tasks are mostly short-answer.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a single stated confidence for pass/fail decisions.

source: Xiong et al. (2024), consistency across samples
finding: Agreement among several sampled answers predicts failure much better than verbalized confidence, especially on arithmetic. Gains rise with sample count and then flatten.
numbers: 5 samples with consistency aggregation lifted GSM8K AUROC from 54.8% to 92.7%.
limits: Cost scales with samples; gains are smaller on knowledge tasks than arithmetic.
agent_relevance: Use agreement across about five independent samples as the confidence signal, computed by the program.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration (EMNLP)
finding: For RLHF models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2) verbalized confidence is often better calibrated than token probabilities. Asking for several answer guesses before the confidence improves calibration, framed as 'considering the opposite' from psychology.
numbers: TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA. With temperature scaling, verbalized methods often cut ECE by over 50% versus conditional probabilities.
limits: ECE alone ignores discrimination; Xiong et al. (b08) find weaker AUROC for similar methods. Different datasets and metrics explain part of the tension.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt step: list several candidate answers before stating confidence. Always fit a rescaling on held-out data.

source: Guo et al. (2017) On calibration of modern neural networks
finding: Modern deep nets are more miscalibrated than older ones. Temperature scaling, a single-parameter post-hoc fix, beat the other tested methods on most datasets. Defines the binned ECE used in most LLM calibration work.
numbers: ECE = weighted average over M bins of |accuracy - confidence|.
limits: Image and text classifiers, not generative LLMs. ECE depends on binning.
agent_relevance: Cheapest repair: fit a rescaling constant on held-out items and map stated confidence through it.

source: Kuhn, Gal & Farquhar (2023) Semantic uncertainty (ICLR)
finding: Entropy over meaning clusters of sampled answers (semantic entropy) predicts correctness better than sequence entropy, length-normalised entropy, lexical similarity and p(True). The advantage grows with model size.
numbers: Measured by AUROC on TriviaQA and CoQA; figure axes span roughly 0.68 to 0.80 (read from plots, not tables).
limits: Needs several samples and a meaning-equivalence check; short factual answers. The later Nature version (Farquhar 2024) was not opened.
agent_relevance: A program can cluster sampled answers by equivalence and use cluster mass as confidence, matching the rule that code decides.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky & Hashimoto (2024) Relying on the unreliable
finding: Deployed LMs rarely express doubt even when wrong. When prompted for confidence they are overconfident. In user studies people rely heavily on LM output whether or not it is marked with certainty or doubt.
numbers: Average 47% error rate among confident responses.
limits: Only abstract-level figures recorded for the human experiments.
agent_relevance: A stated 'I am sure' from our agent is not a safe signal. Map stated confidence through a measured calibration table.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What LLMs know and what people think they know (Nat. Mach. Intell.)
finding: Calibration gap and discrimination gap between model confidence and the confidence people place in its answers. Default explanations make people overconfident. Matching the explanation's uncertainty wording to the model's confidence narrows both gaps.
numbers: 301 participants, 40 questions each. Model AUC: GPT-3.5 .751, PaLM2 .746 (multiple choice), GPT-4o .781 (short answer). Human AUC on default explanations: .589, .602, .592. Uncertainty wording low vs medium vs high: BF>100.
limits: Crowd participants, MMLU subset, 2023-2024 models. The explanation selection rule was tuned on the same data.
agent_relevance: Wording moves reader confidence strongly, so wording must follow measured confidence.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025), explanation length and expertise
finding: Longer explanations raised human confidence without helping people tell right from wrong. Self-rated topic expertise did not help either.
numbers: Long versus short explanation: BF=25 for higher confidence; mean participant AUC .54 (long) and .57 (uncertainty-only), BF=.23. Higher self-rated expertise: AUC .600 vs .579 (BF<1), ECE .289 vs .292.
limits: Self-rated expertise from a brief survey, 10 MMLU topics.
agent_relevance: Length is a false confidence cue. Keep explanations short; never use length to signal certainty.

source: Steyvers & Peters (2025) Metacognition and uncertainty communication in humans and LLMs
finding: Review of LLM metacognition against human work. Explains meta-d' as the sensitivity measure not contaminated by performance, separates calibration from discrimination, and lists parallels (overconfidence in both) and differences. Notes that human sensitivity improves with feedback and that LLM metacognition can be tuned by training objectives.
numbers: Example LLM discrimination values cited: AUC 0.778 and 0.83, described as modest separation.
limits: Review; many cited studies not opened here.
agent_relevance: Report bias, calibration and sensitivity apart. Feedback is the human intervention that works.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning models better express their confidence (NeurIPS)
finding: Six reasoning models were better calibrated than non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings. Calibration improves as the chain of thought unfolds, a trend not seen in non-reasoning models. Prompting non-reasoning models to slow-think also helps.
numbers: GLM-Z1 vs GLM-4 on NonambigQA: 0.07 lower accuracy but 0.037 lower ECE and 0.078 higher AUROC.
limits: Knowledge QA; some non-reasoning models beat reasoning ones on AUROC.
agent_relevance: Calibration is not just a by-product of accuracy; use extended checking before stating confidence.

source: Yoon et al. (2025), ablation of slow-thinking parts
finding: Removing exploration of alternatives or epistemic phrases from the chain of thought hurts calibration. Removing explicit reasoning about confidence changes little, so gains come from thinking about the question, not about confidence.
numbers: TriviaQA (ECE/AUROC): original 0.042/0.782; minus confidence reasoning 0.063/0.763; minus epistemic markers 0.109/0.837; minus non-linear reasoning 0.161/0.734; no CoT 0.150/0.689.
limits: One reasoning model on two datasets for the ablation.
agent_relevance: Order the steps: verify and try alternatives first, then state confidence. Do not add a separate reflect-on-confidence step.

source: Yoon et al. (2025), AUROC artefact from coarse confidence bins
finding: A model using only two confidence values (95% or 65%) can score higher AUROC than one with a finer spread while having worse ECE. The two metrics can disagree.
numbers: TriviaQA without epistemic markers: ECE 0.042 to 0.109 but AUROC 0.782 to 0.837.
limits: A metric quirk, not extra knowing.
agent_relevance: Check both metrics and the number of distinct confidence values before accepting a calibration claim.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) LLMs must be taught to know what they don't know (NeurIPS)
finding: Prompting alone does not calibrate open-ended answers. Fine-tuning with LoRA on about a thousand graded correct and incorrect answers gives a confidence estimate that beats baselines and generalises, even across models.
numbers: Prompted methods: ECE does not improve as the base model improves; AUROC rises only slightly; even the best prompted model trails the worst fine-tuned model (LLaMA-2 7B). Token perplexity does not predict correctness on open-ended MMLU.
quote: a thousand graded examples are sufficient
limits: Needs open weights and training.
agent_relevance: If we fine-tune a small head, about 1000 graded items is enough. Prompt-only systems should expect weak calibration.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024), user study on calibrated scores
finding: People use reliable confidence scores when deciding whether to accept an LLM prediction, and ignore random scores.
numbers: N=181 crowd participants, 20 per variant, multiple choice exam with Mistral 7B Instruct; strongest reliance discrimination with LoRA + Probe scores.
limits: Preliminary study, described as such by the authors.
agent_relevance: Calibrated confidence changes reader behaviour only when it is informative.

source: Chhikara (2025) Mind the confidence gap
finding: Across nine LLMs and three QA datasets, adding explicit distractors to the prompt can reduce miscalibration. Large RLHF-tuned models start strong but can get worse; small models gain more. Person-based questions fail most.
numbers: Up to 460% relative accuracy gain and up to 90% ECE reduction (best case, from the abstract).
limits: Maxima are best-case; 'one right plus several wrong' setting.
agent_relevance: Mixed support for a 'consider the opposite' step; test on our model before adopting.

source: Kumaran et al. (2025) Overconfidence in initial choices and underconfidence under criticism
finding: Gemma 3, GPT-4o and o1-preview show choice-supportive bias: when their earlier answer is visible, they resist changing it. They also overweight inconsistent advice relative to consistent advice, which is not Bayesian.
numbers: Change-of-mind rate 32.5% (answer hidden) vs 13.1% (shown), p=0.002. With opposite advice 85.0% hidden vs 39.2% shown. Higher advice accuracy still predicted more change of mind.
limits: Latitude, SimpleQA and GSM-MC items with stated advice accuracy; not free reasoning.
agent_relevance: Hide the first answer from the checker. This supports the rule that a model never grades its own text.

source: Huang et al. (2024) LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: Reported self-correction gains rely on oracle labels that tell the model when to stop. Without external feedback, asking a model to review and revise its answer does not help and often hurts.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic correction (round 0/1/2): GSM8K 75.9/75.1/74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8/38.1/41.8; HotpotQA 26.0/25.0/25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5/91.5/89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0/79.5/80.0; HotpotQA 49.0/49.0/43.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, GPT-4 97.5.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
limits: 2023 models without extended reasoning; three benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Monitoring needs an external check. Keep the program-run verifier as the decision point.

source: Rahnev et al. (2020) The Confidence Database (not opened)
finding: Open pool of human confidence datasets, available for comparing model confidence curves with human norms. The full-text fetch failed, so no figures are recorded.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Possible source of human reference curves for later tests.
